column3: This grant will fund the provision of humanitarian protection to those people who qualify under:The Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS), which provides those put at risk by recent events in Afghanistan with a route to safety. This scheme will prioritise:those who have assisted the UK efforts in Afghanistan and stood up for values such as democracy, womens rights and freedom of speech, rule of law (for example, judges, womens rights activists, academics, journalists); and(ii) vulnerable people, including women and girls at risk, and members of minority groups at risk (including ethnic and religious minorities and LGBT).This scheme will resettle up to 20,000 people at risk, with 5,000 in the first year. Spouses, partners, and dependent children under the age of 18 of identified eligible individuals will be eligible for the scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (ARAP), which went live on 1 April 2021, offers relocation or other assistance to those who served alongside our armed forces in Afghanistan and provided important support to Her Majestys Government defence and security mission there, predominantly those who were employed directly, or in certain special cases via contractors, and who are assessed to be at serious risk as a result of such work. It is available to people regardless of rank or role, or length of time served, and builds on the long-standing support already available. The policy provides for the principal applicant to bring their close family members (spouse and under 18 children) to the UK and significantly expands the eligibility criteria from the previous scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.Plus British Nationals and their close family members relocated from Afghanistan to the UK by HM Government.There are currently approximately 15,000 people in the United Kingdom who will qualify under one of these schemes in this current financial year.

5G RuralDorset will deliver the following:Business models for rural 5G servicesWe will address the cost and design challenges of using common wireless infrastructure at national scale to deliver services to rural communities. This will be evaluated by three service providers and across four different test-beds that respond to the needs of those living, working and visiting rural and coastal regions of Dorset and beyond.Rural 5G Testbed rural communities are poorly serviced by wireless connectivity. We will deploy a wide-area 5G wireless testbed allowing businesses and academia to prove the sustainable commercial case for improved 5G connectivity in rural locations. We will deploy new wireless technology on existing masts and fibre owned and operated by internet service provider Wessex Internet allowing rapid deployment on a significant scale. The resulting connectivity will support uses in agriculture and provide access to digital services tackling rural issues including isolation and social care needs. This will show that existing and new infrastructure can be combined to deliver next generation connectivity more affordably.Connected Coast the UKs coastal regions generate significant economic wealth and support a range of leisure activities that boost health and well-being. But the coast can be very dangerous. There are serious challenges communicating in such regions, with the first responder community and organisations including the RNLI, Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) and General Lighthouse Authority (GLA) having very limited access to digital communications services. We will deploy a 5G services test-bed in the Lulworth Cove area and a further maritime safety test-bed on infrastructure along the coast. We will trial digital applications that engage with the public and improve the responsiveness of emergency services to incidents. We will evaluate the upgrade of existing infrastructure around the coast and develop the social and economic case for deployment, considering additional use cases from tourism and aquaculture to education and healthcare.5G Innovation Testbed We will deploy an advanced connectivity testbed at the heart of Dorset Innovation Park, a Local Enterprise Zone and advanced-engineering centre which already supports large and small companies that develop innovative connected products and services. This testbed will be connected to other sites in the UK and focus on wide-area connectivity solutions for rural and coastal regions. It will support businesses operating in the county and across the supply chain to test and develop products before deployment in a collaborative and secure way in this strategically important location.

"Nature Connection North Dorset will inspire a transformative shift in how communities across north Dorset connect with and care for their natural heritage. Through this flagship project, Dorset Wildlife Trust will empower residents to lead local nature recovery efforts, revitalising wild places, enhancing biodiversity, and deepening public engagement with nature. Over five years, we will deliver hands-on support, training, and community-led grants to help people restore woodlands, wetlands, and green spaces, especially in this nature-depleted area. This project will not only deliver visible environmental improvements but also foster stronger, healthier communities with lasting ties to their natural environment. The legacy we seek is a vibrant, connected network of people and places where nature is valued, nurtured, and sustained. By building capacity and embedding inclusive practices, this project will leave a long-term impact on both people and place, contributing to a more resilient and nature-rich future for north Dorset."

column2: "Dorset History Centre: Past Lives, Future Proofed"
column3: "There has never been a more pressing need for the trusted, authentic voice provided by evidence and lived experience. This £5.6 million project will transform Dorset History Centre into a sustainable, inclusive, and nationally significant archive service. A new repository will secure the long-term preservation of Dorset’s documentary heritage for at least 30 years, while reconfigured and modernised public areas will enhance access, visitor experience, and operational efficiency. The project will deliver a strategic programme to widen participation and representation, initially through partnership with arts and heritage organisations and working with grass-roots organisations representing marginalised communities. Enhanced access to 200 years of Dorset’s extensive Quarter Session court rolls dating from 1709 will open up a major historical resource, while DHC will lead regional knowledge exchange in digital preservation and oral history. Together, these investments will strengthen Dorset’s cultural infrastructure, extend community engagement, and ensure resilient stewardship of the county’s heritage."

column3: The Water Environment Improvement Fund (WEIF) grant is to support the maintenance of partnerships across Englands catchments, primarily to deliver a catchment based approach to water, land and flood management. Partnerships need to consider the targets of the 25 year environment plan, including: clean and plentiful water, thriving plants and wildlife, using resources from nature more sustainably and efficiently, enhancing beauty, heritage and engagement with the natural environment and mitigating and adapting to climate change. This focus will include actions to deliver improvements to the Water Environment (Water Framework Directive) (England & Wales) Regulations 2017 objectives, climate crisis, biodiversity crisis, flood risk, coastal erosion, growing population, plastics and land management delivered through an integrated catchment approach. Managing the water environment (including rivers, lakes, groundwater, estuaries and the sea) can be very complex and requires balancing the priorities and needs of multiple water users, landowners, and organisations with differing roles and responsibilities considering how to maximise natural capital and net gain. Individual grant values range from £3,250 for sub-catchments to £250,000 for the Catchment Based Approach (CaBA) National Support Group (NSG).

"Dorset National Landscape wants to support a more diverse range of people to engage with their local heritage to help heritage thrive, be more resilient, valued and cared for now and into the future. To achieve this ambition, we will drive forward, support and coordinate the growth of a network of trained volunteer Nature Buddies embedded into existing heritage and health organisations. These buddies will provide personalised support to overcome barriers faced to engaging with heritage. Digital access improvements and content creation will see heritage opportunities bought to any setting for varying interests and abilities. Community grants will support capital access improvements, increasing the provision of local, relevant and enjoyable spaces for all to enjoy.  
Nature Buddies, along with the digital and capital access improvements, will be a long-lasting legacy built into the ecosystem of support for people accessing heritage. Heritage will become valued in people’s lives."

"The project will have two outcomes: to collect oral histories from people who were children in WW2 and to dramatise them with young people as a series of short audio dramas. 

Life for children in Dorset during the war was extraordinary, but their experiences are under-recorded. 1944: American troops in their tens of thousands arrive to prepare for D-Day. Tanks and Army vehicles fill every tree-lined street. Commandos scale cliffs by night and sleep in family homes by day. Working with young people from deprived areas, the project team will find people who were children in the war years and record their stories for the Dorset History Centre oral archive. 

This archive material will then be used to make a series of radio dramas for community radio, podcasts and displays. Installed as part of a Nothe Fort exhibition, today's children will be the dramatised voices of young people during WW2."

"This project will commemorate 250 years since the birth of Jane Austen, connecting new audiences with her life and work and in particular, the important connections to Dorset.

Through an exhibition, workshops, school and community outputs, volunteer research projects and a public programme of events and activities, we will explore the role of Dorset within the novels, personal connections between Jane Austen and the County, as well as how this remains relevant for all of us today.

The legacy of this project will be new digital content including an online exhibition on our website and new items added to the online collections database.  We will also continue to provide related resources and workshops for schools, community groups and families as part of our ongoing programme.

We will also develop a new partnership with Jane Austen House that will include collaborative marketing and a shared talks programme."

"Lyme Regis Town Mill is a working water mill restored in the 1990’s run by volunteers and producing stone grown flour, providing workspaces for small businesses and the Malthouse, an arts/community space. Following a Lottery funded 2021 independent appraisal we want to provide new activities and inclusive opportunities for local organisations and individuals, who have already indicated support, recruit new volunteers and continue the mill's 'free to visit' model.
Our proposals will implement new interpretation and physical, artistic designed improvements, ensuring this heritage asset is preserved and sustainably enhanced, ensuring a high-quality presentation to visitors. The carbon reduction projects will generate free electricity and improved efficiency of the mill's hydro-electric unit. 
They will also enhance community well-being, benefit the local economy, and provide new volunteering and engagement opportunities for marginalised groups and individuals. The financial resilience of the Trust and the artisan-based makers at the site will be improved."

column2: "Plantlife Ryewater Farm Nature Reserve extension - Land purchase and establishment for conservation"
column3: "This project will allow Plantlife to expand one of its core grasslands nature reserves by acquiring an adjacent area of 1.8ha. This purchase, the associated initial capital works and our long-term commitment to its future management will allow us to bring this land into favourable condition. We will be able to directly contribute to restoring England’s species rich grassland. Acquisition of this extension to our existing reserve at Ryewater Farm is a cost-effective and efficient way to extend appropriate management. This land is within the same SSSI and can be classified as the same grassland habitat to that of Ryewater Farm. Plantlife’s acquisition of this land would offer potential for grassland recovery, improving and enhancing it to the same standard as that of the land already in the charity’s management. This project will extend the area that can be used for access and engagement activities in the future."

column3: "Having established a Youth Panel during the Test phase, Butterfly Conservation (BC) enters the ‘Grow’ phase in a stronger position to tackle our workforce challenge: the under-representation of young people (14-25 years of age) among our volunteers. The Youth Panel will lead our approach to the engagement of young people, tackling how to involve them in our work through new volunteering opportunities and how to retain their interest and support. Having tested different ways of working with our Panel and now understanding the processes we need to underpin this work, we are poised to implement the actions identified by the Panel. The legacy of this project will be the permanent fixture of a Youth Panel within the organisation, new ways of working for our staff and a growing and thriving (and increasingly diverse) young volunteer workforce that bolsters our ability to deliver our strategic aims."

column2: "ST THOMAS'S CHURCH MELBURY ABBAS ROOF REPLACEMENT"
column3: "The church roof is covered with clay tiles. The tiles on the southern aspects of the roof are in reasonable condition but many of the tiles on the northern aspects of the roof have degraded significantly. Clay tiles are particularly vulnerable to frost damage on north facing roof slopes. Over past decades, it has been possible to replace individual damaged tiles but now so many are damaged that this is no longer sensible or cost effective. Both the most recent Quinquennial Reviews [in 2015 and 2020) have recommended that the north facing parts of the roof be stripped and the tiles replaced. Our project aim is to replace the northern aspects of the church roof and keep the buckets out of St Thomas's!"

column2: "Dorset Museum & Art Gallery roof replacement and reimagining of Victorian Hall"
column3: "This project would replace the roof of the Victorian Hall and enable collections currently in storage, to be on public display.  We will be able to again tell the local story of Dorchester and the significance of the origins of Dorset Museum & Art Gallery.  We know our local audiences are disengaged with Museum, many no longer visiting, as this element had to be removed from the previous large capital project, due to escalating costs.  The roof also covers the library that includes many rare books, and staff offices.  All of these areas will be better protected, environmentally sustainability will improve and our running costs will be reduced due to improved performance of the building.  We will also remove inappropriate roof materials, ensuring an appropriate solution for the listed building."

column2: "St. Bartholomew's Church, Dorset - Owen Jones Wall Paintings Restoration"
column3:
"This project for St. Bartholomew's Church, Sutton Waldron, Dorset. It's purpose is the restoration and repair of the interior wall paintings and extending their awareness across all society. They were designed by Owen Jones - influential design theorist of the 19th century, seminal publisher of The Grammar of Ornament, interior designer of the 1851 Great Exhibition, pivotal creator of the Victoria and Albert Museum. Our polychromatic decorations are of major national importance. Originally completed in 1847, it is probably the only example of Jones' designs prior to their use in The Great Exhibition. It is also the last surviving example of a complete Jones' church interior.
The work required, determined by an exhaustive evaluation process, consists of:
Eliminating cause of damp in the west end of the church (tower area).
Restoring decorations affected by the damp and elapsed time,
Restoring ancillary paintwork affected by the damp and wear and tear."

"Our project aims are-
1.	To foster the heritage sector in Dorset through supporting community heritage and local history groups with expertise and resources and support Dorset Council and others in their heritage work.
2.	 To ensure the sustainability of our organisation, by increasing the diversity, numbers and skills of members targeted at disadvantaged people, and procuring much needed equipment
3.	To widen understanding and appreciation of Dorset’s heritage through specific site/community based archaeological surveys and excavations, particularly by under-represented groups.
4.	To  protect the heritage at specific sites through improved understanding and care by the local community, community groups and historic asset owners through engagement and management plans.
5.	To impact the mental and physical health of participants positively."

"Our project will prepare Shire Hall Museum for an economically viable future focused on the needs of our visitors and community. 
We will do this through the following: 
•	Undertake visitor research to better understand our visitors and non- visitors and their expectations and needs 
•	Produce a new business plan having explored new operating models and ways to attract audiences both in person and digitally. 
•	Create a marketing and PR plan that will enable growth and help us connect with more diverse audiences so that the stories we tell can have a wider reach.
•	Upgrade our website to interact effectively with our back office providing more opportunities to develop digital content with greater accessibility and integrated customer relations management. 
•	Expand our community engagement offer focusing on engaging younger generations with learning about the importance of social justice, growing our volunteer workforce and developing community co-creation opportunities."

column2: "How to Become A Peregrine - Exploring the Legacy of JA Baker's The Peregrine"
column3:
"Our organisation with 30 young people from deprived and rural wards in Dorset bring to life the pioneering field study and writing of disabled ornithologist/ conservationist JA Baker on the centenary of his birth in 1926. 
Collaborative workshops lead to a digital legacy of Baker’s seminal text - The Peregrine (1967) including 4 large scale illustrated montage panels depicting scenes from the book to be showcased at our Winter shows in 2025 with prints donated to University of Essex and Durlston Country Park for posterity. A digital legacy includes a webpage of the panels and a film of the workshop participants contributing to the illustrated panels and to a live score. Produced by award-winning BBC producer Sarah Cuddon and director of Cabinet of Living Cinema, Kieron Chissik, this legacy project celebrates Baker's groundbreaking nature writing and invites young people to be enthralled by nature writing, birdlife and green spaces."

"Bridport Museum Trust has been offered a unique opportunity to acquire and save for the community a landmark building, the Grade II* Bridport Literary and Scientific Institute (LSI). This potentially transformational offer from the Bridport Area Development Trust presents the Museum with the chance to marry its three key strategic objectives as it approaches its Centenary in 2032: to develop a sustainable operating model; to secure a fit for purpose collection store; and to ensure we have a refreshed and relevant proposition for the future. 
The legacy of the project will be greater organisational resilience through creating a business plan that draws on engagement with our communities. The related collections development will revitalise our relevance and deepen our connection with audiences as we approach our Centenary. In addition, if due diligence supports taking on the LSI building, this would address collection storage and safeguard the LSI for the community."

column2: "The Literary and Scientific Institute (LSi) project requires emergency funding for urgent repairs and maintenance to ensure the future sustainability of the Georgian Style building."
column3:
"Bridport Area Development Trust (BADT) want to ensure a watertight Literary & Scientific Institute (LSi) Building that is fit for climatic conditions by undertaking remedial works to the existing parapet gutter to the front roof slope, form an opening through the end gable to allow water to discharge into the new downpipe ~ this is currently seen as the most appropriate long term solution to avoid taking rainwater back through the roof space and to the rear gutter as happens at present. 
This project will subsequently enable BADT to complete the insurance repairs to the Top and First Floor offices ceilings in security and safety and protect them from future leaks. 
This in turn will enable us to consider a transfer of ownership to the Bridport Museum Trust. (126 words)"

column2: "Flax Forward - From land to linen and beyond - Telling the story of a plant, a town and a landscape."
column3:
"This community-led project will celebrate Bridport’s flax-growing heritage while exploring the potential of locally grown, natural materials for a sustainable future.
The project will seek out, gather and collate knowledge from heritage collections, archives and a wide range of community sources. Kickstarted through a community research phase we will uncover lost flax infrastructure, memories, and oral histories. Adding to heritage data and making the story of Flax in the Bridport Area more accessible. 
Alongside community research we will provide hands-on, practical education in the cultivation and processing of flax. Community volunteers will work together to design and make a “Bridport Dress” using locally grown and processed Flax. 
Exhibitions and events will celebrate heritage and share it with wider audiences. By combining practical craft with heritage research and creative interpretation, the project will strengthen connections between people and their town highlighting how understanding the past can inspire the present."

"'Bubbles and Squeaks' will celebrate and draw public attention to 3 West Dorset rivers, the Mangerton, Cerne and Hooke. 

Emerald Ant, our partners and schools, want to support children and young people to be future environmental stewards, by building a greater appreciation and love for our local rivers, inspiring others to act, and encouraging action within communities. 

We want to equip children and young people with:

- a holistic appreciation of local rivers and their landscape, understanding geology, geography, the resources and habitats waterways provide for wildlife, and the human relationships we have with rivers as places for settlement, food, power, and outlets to the sea.
-a greater understanding of local history; connections between rivers, settlements and place names
- a desire to reduce the pressures on our rivers and chalk streams

Schools and communities will create a body of large-scale celebratory 'river-life' for 3 highly artistic, inspiring riverside events."

"We want to establish a sustainable and successful museum for Weymouth, based in the historic heart of our vibrant town.
The museum will showcase our rich and diverse social history, fine art, textile and maritime collections, which are currently at significant risk. 
We will create immersive and accessible interpretation within a landmark heritage building, which has previously been in a state of dereliction and is currently benefitting from £28 million of private sector investment. 
We will deliver an exciting visitor offer and community curated spaces which truly reflect, represent and celebrate the lived experiences of local people. 
Our legacy will be to establish Weymouth’s first, designed for purpose, community museum with cultural facilities and programming predicated on enriching the lives of our local residents to foster pride and belonging in Dorset Council’s largest and most demographically diverse urban conurbation."

column2: "Bridging the Gap: Making Swanage Railway fit for the future."
column3:
"Swanage Railway has limited accessibility to its carriages for visitors who are wheelchair users or who have other physical disabilities and issues. We currently have a wagon that has been adapted which can be accessed by a ramp, but this does not provide equality of access or experience, and lack of seats means that those travelling in groups have to be separated on occasions. 

As well as accessibility for our public services, a learning and community engagement programme is being developed and for its successful delivery, it is essential that we have accessible carriages for visitors available at all times as well as for special events and projects. 
Swanage Railway is committed to consulting and engaging with disabled communities in Purbeck and wider Dorset in new, creative and innovative ways which this project funding will allow us to fulfil."

"Through this project, the Museum of East Dorset will become a more resilient, sustainable and inclusive organisation, better able to care for the heritage of East Dorset's people, villages and towns. We’ll deliver a diversified Fundraising Plan, modernise back-office digital systems, install solar PV and removable secondary glazing to cut carbon and running costs, and recruit a Community Engagement Manager to reach the most vulnerable in our community: isolated older residents, families on low incomes, and those underserved by heritage.

The project underpins our new three-year Business Plan, creating a financially and environmentally sustainable museum with diverse audiences, lower operating costs, increased fundraising income, and the organisational capacity to protect our local heritage long-term.

The project’s legacy will be a vibrant museum deeply rooted in its community, with the resilience to flourish despite the challenging external environment and trusted as a place where local heritage drives wellbeing, learning and pride."

30-bed critical care unit, which will become one of the largest in the country. However, the critical care unit 
will be on the first floor, which will make the outdoors inaccessible for staff and patients. This is because 
the hospital green spaces are situated a five-minute walk from the unit, which would compromise the swift 
response needed in the instance of a patient health emergency.
However, our planned approach to this problem is to transform a 200m2 unused balcony into a Critical 
Care Wellbeing Garden. The balcony is situated next to the critical care unit, so patients can be wheeled on 
their beds into the garden to reap the benefits of nature. Furthermore, it would benefit staff as it is situated 
next to the staff rest room, which would enable them to take a restorative break outdoors.

column3: Build skills and confidence Low confidence is a major factor in poor mental health, often the two become entwined so the worse your mental health is the worse your confidence becomes and vice versa. In our support groups we have a tried and tested program for helping building self-esteem among women. We ask women to think about what is affecting your self-esteem. We work on avoiding negative self-talk. We encourage connecting with people who love you. We do resilience based education to help women to become more assertive. We teach skills to help with self-care and our group members are set challenges which are all about focusing on the positives. Most importantly the group works together to support each other. Improve health and well-being Our groups are facilitated by a trained mental health counsellor who uses a number of techniques and therapies to help the women improve their mental health. Often just having a safe place to go and discuss freely the challenges they face with other women who have had similar experiences can help. We also when required signpost women to other more appropriate services. Build social networks for women and girls The primary objective of our groups is about connecting with others to reduce isolation. As part of our program alongside the talking element engage in activities and team projects such as arts and crafts. The group also has monthly outings together. These activities help the group to form friendships and a social support network. Many of the women remain friends. The impact of being part of such a group can be life changing for someone with a mental health condition. We see vast improvements participants in regards to improved confidence and social skills and self management of their mental health.

column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

The VPRS scheme has been expanded to meet a commitment made by the former Prime Minister, and is being run by a tri-partite team of officials (the Syrian Resettlement Programme) from the the Home Office and the departments for International Development and Communities and Local Government. This team sits within the Resettlement, Asylum Support and Integration Direcorate in UK Visas and Immigration. This team also has responsibility for running the Vulnerable Childrens Resettlement Scheme.As such, this funding is to be used to meet a government commitment, rather than a Home Office strategic priority. Three key objectives have been set for the schemes: resettling Syrian refugees in a way that:Secures and Protects the vulnerable persons and the UK, andHas the Well-being of the vulnerable persons and the welcoming communities at the centre of decision making, andDelivers value for money for the UK tax payer.This grant is primarily designed to assist with promoting refugee well being, whilst ensuring value for money. It is designed to contribute to costs incurred for the first year that beneficiaries spend in the UK for primary and secondary health care costs.The VPR scheme was upscaled in September 2015 to meet commitments made by the former Prime Minister, including to resettle 1,000 Syrians by Christmas 2015. In view of the scale of the challenge and limited time available, the Home Secretary authorised the formation of a Gold Command Structure, which provided the designated Gold Commander (Paul Morrison) with high-level Ministerial authority to make the necessary funding and operational decisions to deliver these commitments. The VCRS scheme was announced in April 2016 and utilises the same delivery partners.Since then the formation of the Gold Command, the Programme  which operates both schemes  has had regular contact with Ministers at Secretary of State level. column3: This grant will fund the provision of humanitarian protection to those people who qualify under:The Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS), which provides those put at risk by recent events in Afghanistan with a route to safety. This scheme will prioritise:those who have assisted the UK efforts in Afghanistan and stood up for values such as democracy, womens rights and freedom of speech, rule of law (for example, judges, womens rights activists, academics, journalists); and(ii) vulnerable people, including women and girls at risk, and members of minority groups at risk (including ethnic and religious minorities and LGBT).This scheme will resettle up to 20,000 people at risk, with 5,000 in the first year. Spouses, partners, and dependent children under the age of 18 of identified eligible individuals will be eligible for the scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (ARAP), which went live on 1 April 2021, offers relocation or other assistance to those who served alongside our armed forces in Afghanistan and provided important support to Her Majestys Government defence and security mission there, predominantly those who were employed directly, or in certain special cases via contractors, and who are assessed to be at serious risk as a result of such work. It is available to people regardless of rank or role, or length of time served, and builds on the long-standing support already available. The policy provides for the principal applicant to bring their close family members (spouse and under 18 children) to the UK and significantly expands the eligibility criteria from the previous scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.Plus British Nationals and their close family members relocated from Afghanistan to the UK by HM Government.There are currently approximately 15,000 people in the United Kingdom who will qualify under one of these schemes in this current financial year.

Principle 1 of this strategy states that Local Authority HERs should be the first point of call for and primary trusted source of investigative research data and knowledge. A key output of the project will therefore be a full, structured, electronic catalogue which will promote quick and efficient identification and retrieval of relevant parts of the archive. 2) Conservation and preservation An important counterpart to the catalogue description of the archive is the work that will be undertaken to conserve and promote its long-term preservation. Boy Child Boy Child is a project exploring perceptions of and attitudes towards maleness, the impact of science on male roles and gender, sexual and gender identities in contemporary society, and current concerns with regard to health in the male population as well as the science of memory and the prism through which individuals see their own history. Drawing on the stories of seven males, from birth to old age, the project will engage male children at a secondary school, a feeder primary school, excluded young males, prisoners, health service staff and older men in developing performance, film, sculpture and installation pieces in response to the seven stories. The process will be collaborative involving the documentation of personal histories and experience through performance and oral history techniques. Building on the experience of creating site specific performance in Visiting Time (a research project funded through the first PULSE award) Boy Child will result in seven pieces of work, created as independent site specific events, and then brought together, after a further development phase, into a larger scale event aimed at a wider audience. The project aims to: Draw out issues of science relevant to the ordinary lives of individuals through the stories of seven people and explore these through connections to the experience and understanding of participants. Raise awareness of and engage participants in investigating issues of maleness in relation to science, gender roles, genetic inheritance, health, and contemporary society. Explore intergenerational and science issues around changing roles and memory. Develop an innovative cross art-form process, which draws on individual experience and understanding and places the participants at the centre. Use participatory activities to explore different contexts for male experiences and attitudes in relation to contemporary male identity (such as at primary school, during puberty, paternity, an all male environment - prison). Build on the experience and learning of Visiting Time. Communicate issues of maleness and science through experimental and challenging performance and cross arts media, to a wide audience.

Visiting Time Visiting Time is an exploration of the human, experiential and scientific dimension of children living with genetically inherited disorders. It is a research and development project which will explore the feasibility of using participatory, site-specific performance practice to engage young people, patients and a hospital community in broadening understanding of genetically inherited disorders and the role of bio-medical science in their treatment. Visits to GP surgeries, consultants and the hospital's pathology laboratory will inform the scientific research which will be led by AS level Science students. This information will in turn inform a series of drama based activities with Year 9 students which will explore the research material and investigate the possibilities of developing site-specific performance in environments such as healthcare buildings, hospitals and GP surgeries. The development phase will allow for an exploration of the possibility of involving young people attending Dorset County Hospital, through the school in the children's ward, and in consultation with hospital staff and parents. The evidence emerging from the research phase will be published in a report and discussed with healthcare professionals, artists, educationalists and participants. This process will then form the foundation for the development of a site-specific performance event for which further funding will be sought.

column3: This two-year project is for disabled people in Bournemouth. It aims to improve social connections by creating social links, developing peer support opportunities and improving mental and physical health. It provides a series of social and vocational activities with a range of options including Pilates, yoga, walking, woodwork, gardening etc.

This two-year project is for adults with learning disabilities in Weymouth and Portland and Bridport. It aims to build social connections among participants, reducing the isolation they experience as well as building their employability skills. It provides fortnightly friendship clubs with activities chosen by participants such as quizzes, games, walks and dance sessions.

This two-year project creates weekly social activities and lunches for people with disabilities, living in Bournemouth. The project offers a safe and supportive environment in which participants can come together for social interaction and develop confidence, self-esteem and independent living skills as well as improving mental and physical health. Sessions include activities that are determined by participants such as tai chi, yoga and arts and crafts. Each session ends with a shared meal and gives participants the chance to develop friendships and peer support and in an informal setting. Participants shape ongoing delivery through regular feedback sessions.

This two-year project delivered ‘Speaking Up’ and action groups for people with learning disabilities living in Weymouth and Portland in Dorset. Sessions supported people to enhance their confidence and skills to speak up about issues affecting their lives and to voice these issues to key local decision-makers. The VPRS scheme has been expanded to meet a commitment made by the former Prime Minister, and is being run by a tri-partite team of officials (the Syrian Resettlement Programme) from the the Home Office and the departments for International Development and Communities and Local Government. This team sits within the Resettlement, Asylum Support and Integration Direcorate in UK Visas and Immigration. This team also has responsibility for running the Vulnerable Childrens Resettlement Scheme.As such, this funding is to be used to meet a government commitment, rather than a Home Office strategic priority. Three key objectives have been set for the schemes: resettling Syrian refugees in a way that:Secures and Protects the vulnerable persons and the UK, andHas the Well-being of the vulnerable persons and the welcoming communities at the centre of decision making, andDelivers value for money for the UK tax payer.This grant is primarily designed to assist with promoting refugee well being, whilst ensuring value for money. It is designed to contribute to costs incurred for the first year that beneficiaries spend in the UK for primary and secondary health care costs.The VPR scheme was upscaled in September 2015 to meet commitments made by the former Prime Minister, including to resettle 1,000 Syrians by Christmas 2015. In view of the scale of the challenge and limited time available, the Home Secretary authorised the formation of a Gold Command Structure, which provided the designated Gold Commander (Paul Morrison) with high-level Ministerial authority to make the necessary funding and operational decisions to deliver these commitments. The VCRS scheme was announced in April 2016 and utilises the same delivery partners.Since then the formation of the Gold Command, the Programme  which operates both schemes  has had regular contact with Ministers at Secretary of State level. They are aware of our choice of delivery partners and funding model.The VPR and VCRS schemes are being evaluated through a programme of data monitoring and qualitative research and this will include examining some VFM considerations.

On 7 September 2015 the serving Prime Minister announced the expansion of existing UK resettlement schemes to resettle up to 20,000 Syrian refugees under a new Vulnerable Person Resettlement Scheme (VPRS) by 2020. The scope of this Programme was expanded in July 2017 to include the most vulnerable refugees in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region who have fled the Syrian conflict, regardless of nationality.In April 2016 a further commitment was made to resettle up to 3,000 children and their families from the (MENA) region over the same period under the Children at Risk UNHCR vulnerability category, the Vulnerable Children Resettlement Scheme (VCRS).This grant stream is for the provision of post-arrival services to refugees resettled in the UK under these schemes through tariff/per capita payments.At present the majority of arrivals are being supported by local authorities and the funding provides an un-ringfenced contribution to their costs.Payments may also be made for some local authority services for families resettled under the Community Sponsorship scheme which the Home Secretary announced in July 2016.Payments are also made for the same purpose to Horton Housing Association.The required outcomes include:- The Recipient will arrange accommodation for the arriving Beneficiaries which meets local authority standards, and which will be available on their arrival and is affordable and sustainable.- The Recipient will ensure that the accommodation is furnished appropriately.- The Recipient will meet and greet arriving refugees from the airport and escort them to their accommodation, providing a welcome pack of groceries at their home.- The Recipient will provide an initial cash allowance for each Beneficiary of £200  this is to ensure they have sufficient funds to live on while their claim for benefits is being processed. An additional payment of up to £100 per person may also be paid to local authorities where Universal Credit has been rolled out to cover initial delays in UC payments- The Recipient should ensure that Beneficiaries are provided with a dedicated source of advice and support to assist with registering for mainstream benefits and services, and signposting to other advice and information giving agencies  this support includes:- Assisting with registration for and collection of Biometric Residence Permits following arrival- Registering with local schools, English language and literacy classes- Attending local Job Centre Plus appointments for benefit assessments- Registering with a local GP- Advice around and referral to appropriate mental health services and to specialist services for victims of torture as appropriate- Providing assistance with access to employment.- The Recipient shall undertake an assessment with each Beneficiary of their English language capability to determine appropriate support arrangements through provision of English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) or equivalent. The purpose of the language tuition is to ensure that each Beneficiary is able to carry out basic transactions within the communities in which they have been placed. Beneficiaries should be able to access such classes within one month of their arrival and they should be made available until such time as suitable mainstream provision becomes available or until 12 months after arrival (whichever is sooner).

column3: We believe that a dedicated volunteer programme has the potential to significantly impact the lives of the most vulnerable women in Bournemouth. Volunteers will build skills and confidence; for example by supporting women to participate in our creative lifestyle sessions, designed to provide opportunities for women to try a new creative hobby or learn a new skill. In addition, current clients who are interested and assessed as suitable will be supported and empowered to become volunteers themselves, benefitting from experience gained and training opportunities available. This could ultimately lead to improved employability skills and job prospects. Female volunteers will support women to improve health and well-being holistically through assisting women to participate in physical activities such as swimming and gardening as well as looking at ways to better look after mental health. At the same time, volunteers will potentially reduce the risk of social isolation with the women they work with by supporting women to build social networks - this could be by accompanying women to Safe and Sound Dorset Creative Lifestyle Sessions or other relevant groups in the community where they can connect with other women and share similar experiences.

column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

column2: Offensive Weapons Act 2019 LA Trading Standards costs
column3: The purpose of the grant scheme is to provide funding to 173 Local Authority Trading Standards departments across England and Wales to meet their responsibilities under the Offensive Weapons Act 2019. The 2019 Act introduced prohibitions on the sale and delivery of corrosive products to under 18s, prohibited delivery of corrosive products to residential premises and lockers in the case of remote sales and also introduced offences on delivery companies in respect of overseas sellers to deliver corrosive products to under 18s at residential premises. Trading Standards are responsible for ensuring that retailers and delivery companies are compliant with their statutory obligations and for the subsequent enforcement of the legislation. The Offensive Weapons Act 2019 also provides investigatory powers for local authorities in relation to enforcement of sales of corrosives.

column2: Afghan Resettlement, Relocation and Integration Support Programme
column3: Local authorities are the main recipients of grant funding in support of those who have been accepted for resettlement and relocation under the Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS) and Afghan Relocation and Assistance Policy (ARAP). Local authority support under these schemes is voluntary and those who agree to support new arrivals to the UK from 01 March 2025 are required to provide time limited integration support in transitional accommodation (up to 9 months) to support beneficiaries to find their own settled accommodation in the UK, develop their English language skills, build self-sufficiency skills and through support and signposting find employment. They will be funded for these activities. For those local authorities who agree to support individuals who settle in their local area, the local authority can claim further funding over the course of the next 3 years to help individuals integrate into communities and continue on their journey to self-sufficiency. This grant stream also includes additional payments, in the first year upon arrival in the UK, to support with education and the provision of healthcare services. The latter are made to Integrated Care Boards and other health bodies in the devolved administrations.

column2: GRCF2021: Court Farm Rewilding Project - delivering nature's recovery and climate resilience
column3: Imagine being able to access a wilderness direct from your front door. Once barren fields, ringed with barbed wire, polluting the waterways and excluding the community, now a restored landscape, alive with returning wildlife, grazing animals and people.Dorset Wildlife Trust has a unique opportunity to establish a large community-based nature recovery project. We have created a new financial model using nature-based solutions to acquire 170ha of low-quality agricultural land in a key location. We will build a Nature Recovery Network in Dorset at a landscape-scale that will help control pollution entering the internationally important Poole Harbour while addressing the climate and ecological crises.The project will establish the UKs first community rewilding project, as well as the first such project in Dorset. We will rewild 150ha including 30ha of new wetlands that restore nature, hold back and cleanse water and capture carbon. The local community will help to create wild areas close to them, including 12.2ha of new community woodlands and orchards. The project will create two full-time jobs and support local contractors in delivering a range of nature-recovery activities.

column2: NCF NCPGS Peatland Restoration Round 3 - Dorset
column3: Project aims:1) To restore 172ha of mire & fen habitat across 16 sites within the Dorset Heaths, through re-establishing natural hydrological processes and promoting the recovery of declining mire vegetation communities to restore the peat-forming and carbon storage functions of these sites. This includes 169.3ha protected sites, kickstarting recovery from unfavourable to favourable condition.2) To foster stewardship of mires and wet heaths among neighbouring communities and visitors, through improved understanding and appropriate involvement in restoration delivery.Restoration objectives:The following objectives relate to restoring the mire habitat itself, and underpin the outcomes we aim to achieve across the sites:1) Hold water on site by blocking artificial drains using peat bunding, spoil infill, notched dams and interrupting former plantation ridge and furrow topography to allow existing surface level groundwater outflows to re-establish naturally higher water levels at or just below the surface.2) Reduce water loss through evapotranspiration by removing trees & scrub and flattening Molinia tussocks, promoting better hydrological conditions for remaining mire specialist plant communities to recover and thrive.

column3: The Water Environment Improvement Fund (WEIF) grant is to support the maintenance of partnerships across Englands catchments, primarily to deliver a catchment based approach to water, land and flood management. Partnerships need to consider the targets of the 25 year environment plan, including: clean and plentiful water, thriving plants and wildlife, using resources from nature more sustainably and efficiently, enhancing beauty, heritage and engagement with the natural environment and mitigating and adapting to climate change. This focus will include actions to deliver improvements to the Water Environment (Water Framework Directive) (England & Wales) Regulations 2017 objectives, climate crisis, biodiversity crisis, flood risk, coastal erosion, growing population, plastics and land management delivered through an integrated catchment approach. Managing the water environment (including rivers, lakes, groundwater, estuaries and the sea) can be very complex and requires balancing the priorities and needs of multiple water users, landowners, and organisations with differing roles and responsibilities considering how to maximise natural capital and net gain. Individual grant values range from £3,250 for sub-catchments to £250,000 for the Catchment Based Approach (CaBA) National Support Group (NSG). Defra sub-outcome: 1.5 Improved access to nature

column3: The purpose of the grant scheme is to provide funding to 173 Local Authority Trading Standards departments across England and Wales to meet their responsibilities under the Offensive Weapons Act 2019. The 2019 Act introduced prohibitions on the sale and delivery of corrosive products to under 18s, prohibited delivery of corrosive products to residential premises and lockers in the case of remote sales and also introduced offences on delivery companies in respect of overseas sellers to deliver corrosive products to under 18s at residential premises. Trading Standards are responsible for ensuring that retailers and delivery companies are compliant with their statutory obligations and for the subsequent enforcement of the legislation. The Offensive Weapons Act 2019 also provides investigatory powers for local authorities in relation to enforcement of sales of corrosives.

This project will examine the health and ill health of the poor in Dorset coastal communities during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Using overseers' accounts. vestry minutes, charity records, friendly society records, the diaries and letters of middling and aristocratic families, and the records of doctors, it will: Seek to quantify the extent of ill-health amongst the poor between 1750 and 1835 Seek to reconstruct the nature of self- help within and between poor families Examine the relationship between the sickness of the poor and the activities of the Old Poor Law and contrast this with other (non-seaside) communities in Dorset. Examine the role of doctors in seaside towns versus other types of community in Dorset. Examine access to institutional provision for the alleviation of sickness in seaside communities. Examine the particular role of middling and aristocratic families and medical charities in addressing the health needs of poor people in coastal communities. Examine the nature of medical practice in seaside communities with particular reference to the relationship between mobile populations and medical practice.

column3: This is a non-ring-fenced new burdens grant for Fire and Rescue Authorities/Services to provide fire national resilience capabilities to help respond to major and complex incidents and help keep the country safe.
Discretionary grant awarded to Fire and Rescue Authorities (FRAs) to help meet exceptional, unforeseen or significant levels of expenditure incurred.

The Grant is being awarded to fire and rescue services (FRSs) to deliver the Communities Secretarys commitment to review all high-rise residential buildings over 18 metres by the end of December 2021. The £6 million of funding will be distributed to FRSs through grant funding using a formula-based funding predicated on the estimated number of high-rise residential buildings in scope for the exercise. Each FRS will receive a minimum of £60,000 (with the exception of the Isles of Scilly and Isle of Wight FRSs owing to the small number of relevant buildings within their areas). An additional £1.1m will be allocated using a formula to FRSs to enable the accreditation and training of fire safety inspectors to increase the protection capability within each FRS and to assist with the delivery of the commitment outlined above. The aims are to ensure that all residents of high-rise residential buildings are safe, feel safe now and in the future following an assessment or audit of all buildings in scope by no later than December 2021. It is anticipated that further funding will be made available in 2021/22 for the second year of the programme but this will be subject to confirmation as part of the Spending Review.

column3: The Wellbeing Workshops will improve health and wellbeing by encouraging clients to develop skills that can be carried forward into their personal lives. Provision of a range of different workshops ensures clients will have a choice and will be able to choose which programme they want to engage with that might be most suitable to meed their own needs or a new interest they wish to pursue. Through engagement in the workshops it is expected that our clients will have a reduced sense of isolation, will be able to develop positive relationships with other members of the group. column3: This grant will fund the provision of humanitarian protection to those people who qualify under:The Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS), which provides those put at risk by recent events in Afghanistan with a route to safety. This scheme will prioritise:(i) those who have assisted the UK efforts in Afghanistan and stood up for values such as democracy, womens rights and freedom of speech, rule of law (for example, judges, womens rights activists, academics, journalists); and(ii) vulnerable people, including women and girls at risk, and members of minority groups at risk (including ethnic and religious minorities and LGBT).This scheme will resettle up to 20,000 people at risk, with 5,000 in the first year. Spouses, partners, and dependent children, under the age of 18, of identified eligible individuals will be eligible for the scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (ARAP), which went live on 1 April 2021, offers relocation or other assistance to those who served alongside our armed forces in Afghanistan and provided important support to Her Majestys Government defence and security mission there, predominantly those who were employed directly, or in certain special cases via contractors, and who are assessed to be at serious risk because of such work. It is available to people regardless of rank or role, or length of time served, and builds on the long-standing support already available. The policy provides for the principal applicant to bring their close family members (spouse and under 18 children) to the UK and significantly expands the eligibility criteria from the previous scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.

column2: RPA FARMING INVESTMENT FUND (Farming Equipment and Technology Fund)
column3: The Farming Investment Fund comprises two different sub-schemes. The Farming Equipment and Technology fund will provide lower value grants towards a specified list of items proven to be effective in raising productivity. The Farming Transformation Fund will provide a more flexible model where applicants can seek higher-value investments into more significant infrastructure and equipment.The FIF sits alongside other schemes such as those providing business advice (Resilience Fund), R&D (Farming Innovation Programme), environmental land management and improved animal health and welfare. It will support farmers adapt and change to deliver on Defras vision for the future of the agriculture sector.It will aim to increase farmers confidence to invest in novel technologies and practices, during a time of significant sectoral and macroeconomic uncertainty.It will support capital investment, to maximise returns through employing the latest technologies and practices.It will support the sector in reducing GHG emissions contributing to Net Zero goals. In addition, it will support improvement in water and air quality.It will support investing and improving animal health and welfare by farmers.The Farming Investment Fund (FIF) is an evolution of the Countryside Productivity Scheme, following the UKs exit from the EU. The development of the fund has drawn on the experience and evaluation of this predecessor scheme and we have made changes to the design to ensure that it will deliver more effectively an improvement in productivity and the environment in the farming and forestry sectors.

column2: Afghan Citizen Resettlement Scheme & Relocation and Assistance Policy
column3: This grant will fund the provision of humanitarian protection to those people who qualify under:The Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS), which provides those put at risk by recent events in Afghanistan with a route to safety. This scheme will prioritise:(i) those who have assisted the UK efforts in Afghanistan and stood up for values such as democracy, womens rights and freedom of speech, rule of law (for example, judges, womens rights activists, academics, journalists); and(ii) vulnerable people, including women and girls at risk, and members of minority groups at risk (including ethnic and religious minorities and LGBT).This scheme will resettle up to 20,000 people at risk, with 5,000 in the first year. Spouses, partners, and dependent children, under the age of 18, of identified eligible individuals will be eligible for the scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (ARAP), which went live on 1 April 2021, offers relocation or other assistance to those who served alongside our armed forces in Afghanistan and provided important support to Her Majestys Government defence and security mission there, predominantly those who were employed directly, or in certain special cases via contractors, and who are assessed to be at serious risk because of such work. It is available to people regardless of rank or role, or length of time served, and builds on the long-standing support already available. The policy provides for the principal applicant to bring their close family members (spouse and under 18 children) to the UK and significantly expands the eligibility criteria from the previous scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.

This measure is the primary Agri-environment-climate funding for England in delivering the Rural Development programme environmental land management priorities and builds on the agri-environment Countryside Stewardship and Environmental Stewardship schemes offered under the previous RD programme.The measure funds activities intended to deliver environmental land management priorities contributing to Englands Biodiversity 2020 goals and legal obligations under the Habitats, Birds and Water Framework Directives and soil commitments made in the Natural Environment White Paper and increase resilience of wildlife, habitats and ecosystems to climate change.Funding is paid according to the payment rate for each option included in the individual agreement, and the area/length/number of the commitment selected and is based on income foregone and additional costs. Agreements can be 5 year multi annual commitments with the option of annual extensions for a further two years. 10 year commitments or longer will be offered in cases where an exception is clearly justified.RPA administers for measures in England.

The Condition Improvement Fund (CIF) is available to eligible academies, voluntary-aided (VA) schools and sixth form colleges to support condition, and a small number of expansion projects, with the focus being to keep school and college buildings safe and in good working order. The priority for the Department for Education (DfE) in administering the fund is to address significant condition needs, that is, keeping education providers' buildings safe and in good working order. This includes funding projects that address health and safety issues, building compliance and buildings in poor condition. The fund also supports a small number of expansion projects. These are for academies, sixth-form colleges and VA schools rated good or outstanding by Ofsted that can demonstrate a need to expand.

column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

column3: Environmental Stewardship is an agri-environment scheme helping to:Improve water quality and reduce soil erosion by encouraging management which can help to meet these aims;Improve conditions for farmland wildlife including birds, mammals, butterflies and bees;Maintain and enhance landscape character by helping to maintain important features such as traditional field boundaries;Protect the historic environment including archaeological features and artefacts.The scheme, which replaces the older Countryside Stewardship and Environmentally Sensitive Area schemes, is composed of two levels: the Entry Level Stewardship (ELS), Organic Entry Level Stewardship (OELS) for Organic farms, Upland Entry Level Stewardship (UELS) comprising the lower levels; and the Higher Level Stewardship (HLS) for the upper level.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 - Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-outcome 1.4

column3: This measure is the primary Agri-environment-climate funding for England in delivering the Rural Development programme environmental land management priorities and builds on the agri-environment Countryside Stewardship and Environmental Stewardship schemes offered under the previous RD programme. The measure funds activities intended to deliver environmental land management priorities contributing to Englands Biodiversity 2020 goals and legal obligations under the Habitats, Birds and Water Framework Directives and soil commitments made in the Natural Environment White Paper and increase resilience of wildlife, habitats and ecosystems to climate change. Funding is paid according to the payment rate for each option included in the individual agreement, and the area/length/number of the commitment selected and is based on income foregone and additional costs. Agreements can be 5 year multi annual commitments with the option of annual extensions for a further two years. 10 year commitments or longer will be offered in cases where an exception is clearly justified. RPA administers for measures in England.

column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.

column2: RPA FARMING INVESTMENT FUND (Farming Equipment and Technology Fund)
column3: The Farming Investment Fund comprises two different sub-schemes. The Farming Equipment and Technology fund will provide lower value grants towards a specified list of items proven to be effective in raising productivity. The Farming Transformation Fund will provide a more flexible model where applicants can seek higher-value investments into more significant infrastructure and equipment.The FIF sits alongside other schemes such as those providing business advice (Resilience Fund), R&D (Farming Innovation Programme), environmental land management and improved animal health and welfare. It will support farmers adapt and change to deliver on Defras vision for the future of the agriculture sector.It will aim to increase farmers confidence to invest in novel technologies and practices, during a time of significant sectoral and macroeconomic uncertainty.It will support capital investment, to maximise returns through employing the latest technologies and practices.It will support the sector in reducing GHG emissions contributing to Net Zero goals. In addition, it will support improvement in water and air quality.It will support investing and improving animal health and welfare by farmers.The Farming Investment Fund (FIF) is an evolution of the Countryside Productivity Scheme, following the UKs exit from the EU. The development of the fund has drawn on the experience and evaluation of this predecessor scheme and we have made changes to the design to ensure that it will deliver more effectively an improvement in productivity and the environment in the farming and forestry sectors.

column3: This measure covers grants for investments in forest area development and improvement of the viability of forests under Countryside Productivity and ESIF Growth Programme. Forest areas supported under this Measure must be managed in accordance with the UKFS. All holdings over 10 ha must have an approved woodland management plan in place. The measure supports investments in modernising forestry technologies; improving resilience, environmental value and mitigation potential of forest ecosystems; achieving nature, biodiversity and wider ecosystem services objectives; adapting to climate change; forest protection; and creating new woodland and forested areas (except short rotation coppice, Christmas trees and fast growing trees for energy production). State or publicly owned land is not eligible for maintenance payments even if the holder is a private body or individual. RPA administers for measures in England.

column3: This measure is the primary Agri-environment-climate funding for England in delivering the Rural Development programme environmental land management priorities and builds on the agri-environment Countryside Stewardship and Environmental Stewardship schemes offered under the previous RD programme. The measure funds activities intended to deliver environmental land management priorities contributing to Englands Biodiversity 2020 goals and legal obligations under the Habitats, Birds and Water Framework Directives and soil commitments made in the Natural Environment White Paper and increase resilience of wildlife, habitats and ecosystems to climate change. Funding is paid according to the payment rate for each option included in the individual agreement, and the area/length/number of the commitment selected and is based on income foregone and additional costs. Agreements can be 5 year multi annual commitments with the option of annual extensions for a further two years. 10 year commitments or longer will be offered in cases where an exception is clearly justified. column2: M11 - Agri-environment- Organic Farming Exchq funded NSA P2
column3: This measure covers Agri-environment-organic farming support. Payments are based on income foregone and, where relevant, additional costs resulting from converting to an organic farming system. There are 5 different conversion payments available for different farming systems: Rotational Land; Improved Permanent Pasture; Unimproved Permanent Pasture; Horticulture; and Top Fruit. This measure aims to fund organic conversion and maintenance by active farmers and builds on existing conversion and maintenance support under the previous RD programme Environmental Stewardship (Organic Higher Level and Entry Level Stewardship) elements. Activities funded under this measure support farmers wishing to convert to and maintain organic farming systems for environmental benefits. Investments contribute to meeting Englands Biodiversity 2020 goals and legal obligations under the Habitats and Species and Water Framework Directives. Support also aims to deliver the main objectives on biodiversity and the water environment (including flood management). RPA administers for measures in England.
